prompt: What is an autonomous system?
hint: Think of who runs it.

choices.text: A router that runs BGP
choices.why: One AS holds many routers, and plenty of them never speak BGP.

choices.text: A block of addresses such as 203.0.113.0/24
choices.why: An AS originates blocks; it is the network, not the addresses.

choices.text: One administration's network and policy
choices.why: Right. The company, ispa and ispb are one each.

choices.text: An OSPF area joined to area 0
choices.why: Areas divide one IGP inside one organisation; an AS is the organisation's whole network.

prompt: Match each AS number to what it is.
hint: Two ranges are reserved, and one of them is for books.

pairs.right: Reserved for documentation, as in this lab

prompt: In ispa's table, `198.51.100.0/25` has next hop `0.0.0.0` and weight 32768. What does that say?
hint: Who put this route into BGP?

choices.text: The route is invalid and will not be used
choices.why: It is marked *>, valid and best.

choices.text: ispa originates it itself
choices.why: Right. 0.0.0.0 means this router, and 32768 is FRR's weight for a route it originates.

choices.text: ispa learned it from a default route
choices.why: A default route is 0.0.0.0/0 as a destination, not 0.0.0.0 as a next hop.

choices.text: It came from ispb with a weight set by ispb
choices.why: Weight never leaves the router that sets it, and the path is empty, so no AS passed it on.

prompt: Before edge was configured, a1's ping to 203.0.113.10 got `Destination Net Unreachable` from 198.51.100.1. Why?
hint: Look at what ispa's table holds.

choices.text: www was switched off
choices.why: A host that is off produces silence or a host error, not a net error from the provider.

choices.text: ispa blocks traffic to customers that pay nothing
choices.why: No policy in the lab blocks traffic; ispa simply has no route.

choices.text: Nobody had announced the company's block
choices.why: Right. 198.51.100.1 is ispa, and its table held two prefixes, neither of them the company's.

choices.text: a1's default gateway was wrong
choices.why: The error came from 198.51.100.1, a1's gateway, so the gateway was working.

prompt: On which TCP port does BGP run?
hint: Three digits.

prompt: edge's summary showed both sessions up for 00:00:05 with `(Policy)` in the state and prefix columns. What was happening?

choices.text: The sessions were still being negotiated
choices.why: Up/Down counts time established, and messages were flowing.

choices.text: Up, but carrying nothing yet
choices.why: Right. A deliberate refusal, until a policy says what may cross.

choices.text: The providers rejected edge's AS number
choices.why: A wrong AS closes the session; these were up.

choices.text: A policy on the providers was blocking edge
choices.why: The word is about edge's own missing policy, in both directions.

prompt: A new BGP neighbour stays in `Active` for ten minutes. Which is the most useful first check?
hint: Active means the connection is not completing.

choices.text: Whether the prefix lists are permitting exactly the right prefixes
choices.why: Prefix lists act on routes once a session exists. This one has not opened.

choices.text: Whether the AS path of the routes is too long
choices.why: No route has been exchanged yet, so there is no path to look at.

choices.text: Whether maximum-prefix has been exceeded
choices.why: That closes a session that already exchanged routes.

choices.text: Whether the neighbour is reachable and TCP port 179 gets through
choices.why: Right. BGP is a TCP connection first; until it completes, nothing else matters.

prompt: A BGP session between routers in two different autonomous systems is called ___, and one inside a single AS is called iBGP.
hint: The opposite of internal.

prompt: For 198.51.100.0/25, edge holds the paths `64502 64501` and `64501`. Which does it choose, and on what grounds?
hint: Nothing before the AS path step was set.

choices.text: `64502 64501`, since it was received first
choices.why: Age is a late tie-breaker. Path length decides first here.

choices.text: `64501`, the shorter AS path
choices.why: Right. It is marked > in edge's table.

choices.text: `64502 64501`, since it crosses more networks and is more reliable
choices.why: BGP does not reward length; it prefers the shorter path.

choices.text: Both, splitting traffic between ispa and ispb
choices.why: Without multipath configured BGP installs one best path, and the kernel shows one route.

prompt: Put these BGP best-path criteria in the order FRR and Cisco check them.
hint: Local decisions first, then the path, then hints from neighbours.
trap: Local preference comes before the AS path: it is how a network overrides path length, which is why prepending does not always work.

prompt: edge's route map `TO-PROVIDER` has one entry: permit routes matching `OURS`. What happens to a route for 198.51.100.0/25 on its way out to ispb?
hint: What happens at the end of a route map?

choices.text: It is denied, because it matches no entry
choices.why: Right. A route that falls off the end of a route map is denied.

choices.text: It is permitted, because nothing denies it
choices.why: The end of a route map is an implicit deny, which is what makes TO-PROVIDER safe.

choices.text: It is sent with the prefix changed to 203.0.113.0/24
choices.why: A route map can change attributes, never rewrite a route into another prefix.

choices.text: It is sent with 64500 prepended
choices.why: Prepending needs a set clause, which TO-PROVIDER does not have.

prompt: ispb sends edge a route for 203.0.113.0/24 with the AS path `64502 64500`. Even with `FROM-PROVIDER` removed, why does edge not use it?
hint: Look for edge's own number.

choices.text: The prefix is longer than edge's own
choices.why: It is the same /24.

choices.text: ispb's weight is lower than edge's
choices.why: Weight is local and does not travel; the route is refused before any comparison.

choices.text: Its own AS, 64500, is in the path
choices.why: Right. A BGP router refuses any path that already lists its own AS.

choices.text: eBGP routes are not accepted for connected networks
choices.why: They would be accepted and lose on distance; here they never get that far.

prompt: After the policy was applied, how many prefixes did edge receive from each provider?
hint: Read State/PfxRcd.

prompt: After `set as-path prepend 64500 64500`, how many AS numbers long is the path ispa sees directly from edge?
hint: The original number plus the two added.

prompt: After the prepend, a1's traceroute to the web server shows four hops instead of three. Which address is new?
hint: Which provider does a1's traffic cross now?

choices.why: That is ispa, a1's gateway, present before and after.
That was edge's ispa-side interface, where traffic arrived before. It is gone from the path.
That is edge's interface on the server's LAN; traceroute does not print it here.
Right. That is ispb, which a1's traffic now crosses on its way in.

prompt: A company prepends its AS three times towards provider X. Provider X gives every route from its customers a local preference of 200 and routes from peers 100. The company is X's customer. What changes at X?
hint: Which step of the list comes first?

choices.text: Nothing: local preference is checked before path length
choices.why: Right. X still prefers its customer's route, prepend or not.

choices.text: X now prefers the path through its peer, which is shorter
choices.why: Only if local preference were equal. Here it is 200 against 100.

choices.text: X drops the route for having a repeated AS
choices.why: Repetition of the sender's own AS is legal; X drops a path containing X's number, not a repeated one.

choices.text: X splits traffic between the two paths
choices.why: The routes differ at the local preference step, so one wins outright.

prompt: After the prepend, a1's requests reach the company through ispb. Through which provider do the server's replies to a1 leave?
hint: Whose table decides outbound traffic?

choices.text: ispb, since replies follow the request's path back
choices.why: IP has no memory of the way a request came. Each direction is routed on its own.

choices.text: ispa, by edge's own table
choices.why: Right. The prepend changed what ispa chooses, not what edge chooses.

choices.text: Both alternately
choices.why: edge installed one best path for 198.51.100.0/25.

choices.text: Neither, the prepend blocks them
choices.why: A prepend lengthens an announcement; it blocks nothing.

prompt: With `EVERYTHING` applied towards ispb, edge advertised three prefixes. Why is that a leak?
hint: What would ispb do with a route to ispa's customers through edge?

choices.text: It offers transit between ispa and ispb
choices.why: Right. The company would become transit between ispa and ispb.

choices.text: It reveals the company's private addresses
choices.why: The two extra prefixes belong to the providers, not to the company.

choices.text: Three is above the maximum-prefix limit
choices.why: The limit set later is 1000, and it applies to what edge receives.

choices.text: It withdraws 203.0.113.0/24 from ispb
choices.why: The company's block is still among the three.

prompt: Which observation showed that ispb did not accept edge's leaked routes?
hint: Look at ispb's view of ispa's customers.

choices.text: edge's advertised-routes listed 3 prefixes
choices.why: That is what edge sent, not what ispb kept.

choices.text: The session to ispb was closed
choices.why: Nothing closed it; the filter dropped the routes quietly.

choices.text: ispb held one path, from ispa
choices.why: Right. One path, from ispa; nothing from edge.

choices.text: a1 could no longer reach the web server
choices.why: Reachability was not tested in that block, and the leak would not have broken it.

prompt: What does `neighbor 192.0.2.2 maximum-prefix 1000` do on edge?
hint: It guards the receiving side.

choices.text: Limits edge to announcing 1000 prefixes at most, towards ispa
choices.why: It counts what edge receives, not what it sends.

choices.text: Closes the session if ispa sends more than 1000 prefixes
choices.why: Right. A safety net against a provider leaking something huge.

choices.text: Keeps the 1000 best routes and drops the rest
choices.why: It does not pick; it closes the session.

choices.text: Sets the session's timeout to 1000 seconds
choices.why: It is a count of prefixes, not a time.

prompt: A customer leaks a peer's routes to its provider. The leaked path is longer than the one the provider has from that peer. Why can the leaked route still win at the provider?
hint: What do providers set for routes from customers?

choices.text: Leaked routes carry a higher MED
choices.why: MED comes after path length, and a higher MED loses.

choices.text: Local preference is checked first
choices.why: Right. That is the commercial preference that turns a leak into an incident.

choices.text: BGP prefers the newest route
choices.why: Age is among the last tie-breakers, and favours the older route.

choices.text: The leaked prefix is more specific
choices.why: The scenario leaks the same prefixes; a more specific one would be a different problem.

prompt: A ROA says AS 64500 may originate 203.0.113.0/24 with maximum length /24. Match each announcement to its validation state.
hint: Check the origin and then the length.

pairs.left: 198.51.100.0/24 from AS 64500, with no ROA covering it

prompt: Under the same ROA, AS 64500 itself announces 203.0.113.0/25. What is the state, and why?
hint: The ROA has a maximum length.

choices.text: Valid, because the origin AS matches
choices.why: The origin is half of the check; the length is the other half.

choices.text: Not found, because no ROA names a /25
choices.why: The /24 ROA covers the /25, so the state is not "not found".

choices.text: Invalid: /25 is past the maximum
choices.why: Right. Covered by a ROA, right origin, wrong length.

choices.text: Valid, because a more specific prefix is preferred
choices.why: Preference is routing; validation is a separate check against the ROA.

prompt: Route origin validation is deployed everywhere, and somebody announces 203.0.113.0/24 with a path that ends in 64500, forged. What stops it?
hint: Which AS does origin validation look at?

choices.text: Origin validation, which rejects it as invalid
choices.why: The origin is the right one, so it validates; the forgery is earlier in the path.

choices.text: The ROA's signature, which covers the whole path
choices.why: A ROA signs a prefix and an origin AS, nothing about the path.

choices.text: Loop detection on every router
choices.why: That drops paths containing the receiver's own AS, which a forged path need not.

choices.text: Filters and monitoring, not origin validation
choices.why: Right. Validating the rest of the path is work in progress.

prompt: The signed record in RPKI that says which AS may originate a prefix, and up to what length, is a ___.
hint: The holder of the block signs it.

prompt: Which of these are part of the company's side of safe BGP in this lesson? Choose all that apply.
hint: Think of what edge sends, receives and publishes.

choices.text: An outbound filter that announces only 203.0.113.0/24
choices.why: TO-PROVIDER, which kept the leak from happening by default.

choices.text: A ROA for 203.0.113.0/24 with origin 64500 and maximum length /24
choices.why: It lets everybody else reject a false origin.

choices.text: maximum-prefix on both provider sessions
choices.why: The guard on what edge receives.

choices.text: Accepting 203.0.113.0/24 from the providers as a backup
choices.why: FROM-PROVIDER denies it on purpose: nobody else tells edge how to reach its own network.

prompt: Put the steps of this lesson's lab in the order they were done on edge.
hint: Session, policy, steering, mistake, repair.
trap: The policy has to come before anything is exchanged at all: without it the sessions showed (Policy) and carried nothing.

prompt: A small company with one provider asks whether it needs BGP for its /24. What does this lesson suggest?
hint: Lesson 15 had an answer for one way out.

choices.text: Yes, because every public block has to be announced by its holder with BGP
choices.why: The provider can announce a customer's block and route it down a static route.

choices.text: Yes, because BGP converges faster than a static route
choices.why: With one link there is nothing to converge to.

choices.text: No: with one way out, a default towards the provider is enough
choices.why: Right. BGP earns its place with a second provider, as in this lab.

choices.text: No, because private ASNs cannot carry a /24
choices.why: ASN ranges have nothing to do with prefix size.

prompt: Before the prepend, a1's traceroute to 203.0.113.10 showed how many hops?
hint: Provider, edge, server.
